raw_response: {"sentences":[{"text":"Leaving Shakespeare and Company behind, we head for the Sorbonne, about a fifteen-minute walk away.","source_id":"GLUE_NAV","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":7},{"text":"As you walk this last stretch, think back over where we started — Pont Neuf, the bridge whose name means New Bridge though it's really the oldest in Paris, the first built here of stone and free of houses.","source_id":"GLUE_REFLECTION","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":7},{"text":"And the tip of the island, where Jacques de Molay, Grand Master of the Templars, was burnt at the stake and cursed the kings as the flames took him.","source_id":"GLUE_REFLECTION","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Now picture a teacher perched on wooden trestles, and his students sitting on bundles of straw they'd hauled in themselves.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"That's how the Latin Quarter became, in the thirteenth century, the centre of learning for all of Western Europe.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"The first official mention of the university — the Universitas Magistrorum et Scolarium Parisiensium — dates from 1221, and back then it had no home at all.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Lessons happened in the open air, on Place Maubert and mainly on nearby rue de Fouarre — 'fouarre' being old French for that straw, which is exactly how the street got its name.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"The brawls and political agitation got so bad that in 1358 the Regent and future Charles V had the street barred with chains at both ends.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"And yet the teachers here were giants — Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, and Brunetto Latini, the master of Dante.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Dante himself came to study on rue de Fouarre in the early fourteenth century.","source_id":"2702cc9b-ec92-4733-b4ee-06bc90cef2a2","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"In 1253, a college opened here, founded by Robert, chaplain and confessor to Saint Louis.","source_id":"347f9ed9-bd0e-449f-b8bb-e5a31a1e5f0f","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Born to a humble family in the village of Sorbon in the Ardennes, Robert became such a scholar that the King had him dine at his own table.","source_id":"347f9ed9-bd0e-449f-b8bb-e5a31a1e5f0f","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"His college became the seat of the faculty of theology, and it took the name of his village — La Sorbonne.","source_id":"347f9ed9-bd0e-449f-b8bb-e5a31a1e5f0f","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"It expanded so spectacularly that it soon overshadowed everything around it, and to this day many foreigners mistake it for the entire University of Paris.","source_id":"347f9ed9-bd0e-449f-b8bb-e5a31a1e5f0f","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Then the Hundred Years' War broke out, and the university — which had slowly lost its old privileges — sided with the English against the King of France, and later against Jeanne d'Arc herself.","source_id":"c13bb8e7-bb17-48c6-acdd-8e8aea8840e7","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Paris lay in ruins, wolves roamed the streets, and the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève had become, as they said, an 'annexe of Oxford.'","source_id":"c13bb8e7-bb17-48c6-acdd-8e8aea8840e7","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Peace came in the end, and in 1437 the university submitted to the secular authority of Charles VII.","source_id":"c13bb8e7-bb17-48c6-acdd-8e8aea8840e7","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Richelieu, who'd been a student here and rose to become its dean, took on the renovation.","source_id":"91c91147-f650-489f-b358-f299d81a8d1a","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"He laid the cornerstone of the chapel in 1635, designed by the architect Jacques Lemercier.","source_id":"91c91147-f650-489f-b358-f299d81a8d1a","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"But his project was purely architectural — the curriculum stayed locked to theology right up until the Revolution.","source_id":"91c91147-f650-489f-b358-f299d81a8d1a","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"That beautiful compound, the work of Lemercier and Le Brun, was handled roughly by the anti-clerical Revolutionaries.","source_id":"91c91147-f650-489f-b358-f299d81a8d1a","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"It was rebuilt and expanded in the nineteenth century, with new faculties of science and letters, inaugurated in 1901 beneath murals by Puvis de Chavannes.","source_id":"91c91147-f650-489f-b358-f299d81a8d1a","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Just over there, Place Maubert — 'la Maube' — had been the haunt of rowdy students and ruffians since the Middle Ages, a place of crime, vice, and public executions.","source_id":"944064cf-3ba4-4598-8ddd-0ef2e5d44805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Erasmus called it 'the cesspit of la Maube,' and by the early twentieth century it was prowled by the terrifying 'Apaches' and their fellow hoodlums.","source_id":"944064cf-3ba4-4598-8ddd-0ef2e5d44805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"In Down and Out in Paris and London, published in 1933, George Orwell described the neighbouring rue du Pot-de-Fer, where he lived at number 6, as 'a ravine of tall, leprous houses, lurching towards one another in queer attitudes, as though they had all been frozen in the act of collapse.'","source_id":"944064cf-3ba4-4598-8ddd-0ef2e5d44805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"And among the destitute Arabs, Poles, and Italians, the respectable French shopkeepers quietly piled up small fortunes.","source_id":"944064cf-3ba4-4598-8ddd-0ef2e5d44805","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"For all these layers, the ground beneath you is older still — the fifth arrondissement holds the longest history of any district in mainland Paris, going back to the Roman occupation of Gaul.","source_id":"c9ed5cdb-2dc0-4836-a4fe-5afb7ea17956","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"When the crowded Île de la Cité spilled onto the left bank, Roman villas rose on the slopes of Mount Leucotitius — the hill we now call the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève.","source_id":"c9ed5cdb-2dc0-4836-a4fe-5afb7ea17956","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"A north-south road, the cardo, ran along what's now rue Saint-Jacques, with a second cardo tracing today's Boulevard Saint-Michel.","source_id":"c9ed5cdb-2dc0-4836-a4fe-5afb7ea17956","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"By the end of the second century this was a neighbourhood of real luxury — the marble and polychrome mosaics dug up on rue de la Harpe prove it.","source_id":"c9ed5cdb-2dc0-4836-a4fe-5afb7ea17956","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"The Romans built three bath complexes here: the northern set at Cluny, the eastern at what's now the Collège de France, and the southern near rue Gay-Lussac.","source_id":"c9ed5cdb-2dc0-4836-a4fe-5afb7ea17956","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"And to feed them all with water, an aqueduct ran the whole way from the Rungis basin, near where Orly airport stands today.","source_id":"c9ed5cdb-2dc0-4836-a4fe-5afb7ea17956","source_type":"beat","stop_idx":7},{"text":"And that brings our walk to a close.","source_id":"GLUE_CLOSING","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":7},{"text":"Thank you for coming along with me today — when you're ready, take your time and keep exploring on your own.","source_id":"GLUE_CLOSING","source_type":"glue","stop_idx":7}]}
